title: New to gamedev, want advice on AI tools for engine, code, and art
author: RuleOverYou15
selftext:
Hey everyone,

Just discovered this sub and I'm blown away by what people are building. I hadn't realised how far AI tooling has come for game dev specifically. I'm a lifelong gamer and software engineer, and it's got me tempted to try making my own game for fun. At work I mainly use Opus models for coding, but I know game dev throws in a whole different layer (visuals, animation, gameplay feel) that's nothing like getting results in a terminal.

Would love to hear what setups have worked well for you:

**Engine choice** – Which of the big three (UE5, Unity, Godot) has the smoothest AI tooling right now? I get that engine choice often comes down to project scope, but I'm just curious what people have had the best luck with.

**Code & scripting** – Which models handle each engine's language best? Not big on C++, so UE5 feels less appealing, but the Blueprints feature looks interesting, how well does that work with AI? And how does AI generated code compare between C# in Unity and GDScript in Godot, is one noticeably more reliable or less error-prone than the other? Also, are there any hidden costs or paywalls around AI features in specific engines?

**Art & sprites** – This is the part I know least about, so any insight helps. How are people handling world building with AI (level layouts, environment design, etc.)? What's working for keeping a consistent art style across assets? Any thoughts on 2D vs 3D when it comes to how well AI handles the asset generation and animation side of things? And for animation specifically, is it mostly still manual, or are people getting decent results with AI there too?

**Sound & music** – Is anyone using AI for SFX or music generation, or is that still mostly manual/asset-store territory? You mentioned art heavily but audio is a whole other lift in game dev people often forget about

I'm just curious what people have had luck with and what things ended up costing them a lot of time. Any advice is greatly appreciated.

comments.author: Seerix
comments.body:
I've had success with Godot. It can run tests and control it pretty well. Seems to have zero issues doing literally exactly what I want with my game. It's a 2.5D isometric space exploration game with fully modular ship building. You control the crew directly (think Xcom style, grid based movement, etc.). Using the ship requires having crew at the appropriate station and spending their turn interacting with it. Salvaging wrecks, exploring old ruins and outposts, crew to crew combat. Each crew member will have their own backstory, attributes, stats, inventory, equipment, etc.

I'm using Astra with blender to create models. It is currently using its own imagegen to create the textures. The models are actually kinda incredible, literally perfect for what I'm doing. For texture work... I wouldn't release it with the current imagegen textures (has that noise pattern that drives me fucking crazy). But I'm also not going to pay someone for texture work until I'm ready to potentially launch the game publically you know? 

As far as worldbuilding and such, it's a proc gen space game. Think starsector kinda? I had it build an editor so I can create new ship parts, modules, systems, points of interest, etc. all in game. Then it's just a matter of lots of play testing until it feels good. 

Sound and music - fuck if i know man, it's just using free shit it found online for now. I'll use 8bit dragon to make some music I gues? but sound effects... no clue.

replies.author: Seerix
replies.body:
Dude I started actively working on it Sunday afternoon and im already at this point. Astra is fucking crazy. Ive had this idea for awhile and I have a good idea of what systems I want in the game and how they will work and interact. Might post some screenshot/video clips later in the week if i can get it to a point im happy with sharing publically. 

But yeah. Combat is xcom like (with less bullshit accuracy rolls lmao). Each crew member gets their own initiative, etc. You can plug AI cores into ship stations(anything that is interactable badically) and that gives *th!/ station* a turn as well. AI cores have random stats just like crew, but they cant gain xp by default. Plugging an AI core into your ships core computer gives the ship itself a turn but people tend to think you are fucking crazy for doing so. Factions/social stuff isnt too fleshed out yet but its coming!

Core gameplay loop is explore, salvage wrecks, upgrade your ship, survive. Will have quests, faction interactions, space station building, kinda sorta 4X mechanics eventually. I want to include planetary exploration eventually but thats like... after 1.0.

comments.author: Both_Lawfulness6708
comments.body:
Claude for coding and reviewing.

Pixellab and aesperite do good retro pixel stuff.

Scenario for more modern looking graphics, it literally has SO many tools and uses.

Suno for background music worked well for me so far.

Eleven labs for sound effects, but, Scenario has an eleven labs sfx tool built in, so, maybe save a subscription.

I'm an outlier here,  and I got an offer for superGrok for $10/ month and figured I'd try it. I've had decent success using it for concept art generation.

It is alot less good for editing, it's a roll of the dice, it tends to change alot even when told not to while editing.

replies.author: Both_Lawfulness6708
replies.body:
It depends.

I think I'll be moving my Strategy game to Godot, but my first simple game I just used HTML and put it in a wrapper when I uploaded it to the playstore.

The biggest AHA moments for me

1. Decide what tools you are using for a said project. Do deep research on their capabilities, verify and add that file in project knowledge while working on your project.

2. Learn to use custom instructions. I have a file I call "How we work" I use, and I keep all.pf these as living documents that I change as we go.

3. Have Claude use other tools via MCP/API.

4. Before I implement any artwork, I asknto see a visual mockup that I verify or deny.

5. I also crested two integrity sweeps that I have Claude run routinely, one to catch bugs, orphaned code etc. And another for art issues.

6. Questions. I like to use the phrase and added it into custom instructions and skills to ask

"What can help me achieve a more desired result, and what questions do you have for me that can achieve a more desired result"
